subject: STRs claim 2-3x the cash flow — here's when that's actually true
preheader: The regulatory wave that killed STRs in dense urban · 4 markets to skip · the operational tax most don't price in

marketSnapshot.headline: STR vs LTR — economics that work in some markets, dead in others
marketSnapshot.body: Short-term rental investing (Airbnb / VRBO model) can produce 2-3x the gross revenue of long-term rentals in destination vacation markets. It also requires operational complexity, regulatory awareness, and risk tolerance that most LTR investors aren't prepared for. The math works in vacation-economy markets. It's killed by regulation in dense urban markets. Knowing which one your specific zip code is in before underwriting is more important than the underwrite itself.

stats.label: Typical STR vs LTR gross ratio

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: STR cap 11% · LTR cap 5.2% · STR wins by 2.1x
dealSpotter.body: Cabin in a vacation-rental destination (Smoky Mountains, Lake Tahoe, Outer Banks, Florida Panhandle). STR projections: $84k/yr gross at 68% occupancy, $42k net after cleaning + dynamic pricing + management. Same property as LTR: $31,800/yr gross, $19k net. STR wins decisively in markets where the local economy IS tourism. The trade-off: cleaning fees, guest-management software, regulatory risk.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: STR was viable · ordinance kills it · WALK
dealSpotter.body: A condo that USED to do $52k/yr as STR until the city passed restrictive ordinance limiting STR to owner-occupant-only for new permits. Existing permits got grandfathered but are non-transferable. Properties without a permit can only operate as LTR — at half the revenue. The same property is a completely different math problem depending on its specific permit status.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: STR allowed but margins thinner · LTR works simpler
dealSpotter.body: A walkable urban neighborhood property where STR is technically allowed but business license required + specific zone restrictions + demand profile is mid-week business mixed with weekend leisure. The STR economics could work — but the LTR economics already work AND require zero operational complexity. Sometimes the answer is 'don't overcomplicate it.'

blogFeature.title: Cash-on-cash vs IRR — what each tells you about a deal
blogFeature.excerpt: STR investors love IRR (captures the full picture); LTR investors lean on cash-on-cash (immediate return on equity). Two metrics, two different stories.

qa.question: Is STR investing still viable, or did regulation kill it?
qa.answer: Both, depending on the market. Regulation killed pure-investor STR in dense urban markets — NYC, LA, San Francisco, Seattle, Asheville, Charleston, parts of Nashville, parts of New Orleans, Maui. In those markets, STR requires owner-occupancy or is banned for non-OO investors. STR is still viable in three categories: (a) destination vacation markets where the local economy IS tourism (Smoky Mountains, Lake Tahoe, Outer Banks, Florida Panhandle beaches, ski towns, Joshua Tree, Sedona) — these markets actively welcome STR. (b) Mid-tier urban markets that still allow it with permit limits (Austin, Atlanta, Phoenix outside Scottsdale — varies block by block). (c) Rural college towns with predictable event-week demand. The right mental model isn't 'STR vs LTR' as a strategy — it's 'this specific zip code right now.' Always check current regulation BEFORE running the STR underwrite. A 5-minute Google search saves you 5 hours of building a model on a deal that can't legally operate the way you assumed.
